lead: The almanac gives high and low water. The rest you work out: the depth at any hour, the water over a sill, the room under a bridge, the stream on each leg.

qa.q: How do I work out the time and height of high water at a secondary port?
qa.a: Apply the **secondary port** differences, with their signs, to the standard port's HW: interpolate the time difference by the standard port's HW time, and the height difference by today's height between neap and spring levels.

blocks.p: On a **semi-diurnal** coast high waters come about 12 h 25 min apart, so tomorrow's tide is some 50 minutes later. **Springs**, the biggest ranges, come a day or two after new and full moon; **neaps** follow the quarters, a week later. Springs grow near the equinoxes and with the moon at perigee.
**Range** = HW − LW of the same tide. Compare it with the mean spring and neap ranges: streams follow the range, not the height of HW. Add the zone to times in UT.

A **secondary port** borrows a standard port's table. Interpolate the time difference by the standard port's HW time between the tabulated times, and the height difference by today's height between neap and spring levels. Apply both with their signs.

sections.title: How much water is really there

qa.q: How do I work out the actual depth of water from the chart?
qa.a: Add the height of tide to the charted depth: both are measured from **chart datum**, about LAT. Over an underlined drying height, the water is the height of tide minus the drying height.

blocks.p: Soundings and tide heights share one zero, **chart datum**, about lowest astronomical tide (LAT). Depth = charted depth + height of tide, so you seldom find less than charted, except on mean-sea-level charts (much of the Med). A minus height dips below datum, and an old chart reduced to MLWS over-reads at big springs. An underlined figure is a **drying height**: water over it = tide − drying height.

fig.note: Underlined: dries 1.8 m above chart datum

blocks.p: MHWS, MHWN, MLWN and MLWS are the mean spring and neap levels. At anchor, depth at low water = depth now − the fall still to come; the next low is lower as springs build. Allow for the sounder's offset and half the swell height in the troughs. Dry out on firm, level ground.

blocks.cap: It falls 3.4 m more: 2.6 m at low water, 0.7 m under the keel.

sections.title: The height between high and low

qa.q: How do I use the rule of twelfths to find the height of tide?
qa.a: Hour by hour from low or high water, the level moves 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1 twelfths of the range: the **rule of twelfths**. Add the rise to LW on the flood; take the fall from HW on the ebb.

blocks.p: Where the tide runs evenly over six hours, the **rule of twelfths** fills the gap: hour by hour the level moves 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1 twelfths of the range, fastest in the third and fourth. Add the rise to LW on the flood, take the fall from HW on the ebb; half an hour takes half that hour's share.

A stand, a double high water or an uneven rise and fall breaks the rule. Use the port's **tidal curve** instead: height = LW + factor × range. Read the spring or neap curve that matches today's range, or interpolate.

qa.q: How much tide do I need to get over a marina sill?
qa.a: The sill's drying height + your draft + a margin. A sill drying 1.8 m, with a 2.0 m draft and 0.5 m to spare, needs a **height of tide** of 4.3 m; then find when the tide reaches it.

blocks.p: Work out the height of tide you need. Over a sill that dries: drying height + draft + margin. Over a bar: draft + margin − charted depth. Then find when the tide reaches it. On the ebb go early: at half tide the level can drop a metre in an hour.

fig.note: Sill dries 1.8 m · you want 0.5 m under the keel

blocks.p: Overhead clearances are charted above HAT, on older charts above MHWS: room now = clearance + that level − height of tide. A surge, or a high water above MHWS, eats into it. Measure to the top of the aerial.

qa.q: How do I read a tidal diamond on the chart?
qa.a: A **tidal diamond** points to a table giving, for each hour from HW at a reference port, the stream's true set and its spring and neap rates. Interpolate the rate by today's range; each row serves half an hour either side.

blocks.p: A **tidal diamond** points to a table: for each hour from HW at a reference port, the set (where the stream goes, true) and the rates at springs and neaps. A row covers half an hour either side of its hour; after HW+6 count back from the next HW. Interpolate between springs and neaps by today's range, extend the line beyond springs, and lay off each hour of a leg in turn.

A **tidal stream atlas** has a page for each hour from HW at its own reference port; 10,22 by an arrow means 1.0 kn at neaps, 2.2 kn at springs. On the chart a feathered arrow is the flood, a plain one the ebb, with the spring rate.

fig.note: Use the nearest diamond in water like yours: here B, not A

sections.title: Where it runs hard, when to go

qa.q: When is the best time to round a headland with a tidal race?
qa.a: At slack water, when the diamond's rate falls to nothing, or pass well outside, above all at night. Off a headland the stream makes a **race** with overfalls, and wind against tide steepens every sea, worst at springs.

blocks.p: Streams run hardest in deep water: mid-channel, in narrows, outside a bend, off headlands. Inshore they are weaker and turn earlier, and a bay may hold an eddy. Against a foul stream, work the edges.

Off a headland the stream makes a **race** with **overfalls**. Wind against tide steepens every sea, worst at springs. Round at slack water, when the diamond's rate falls to nothing, or pass well outside, above all at night. Cross a river bar late on the flood, never on the ebb against a swell.

fig.note: Wind against tide: round at slack, or well outside

blocks.p: A **tidal gate** opens only at a certain state of the stream. Time to leave = time at the gate − distance ÷ speed over the ground. Arrive as it opens; against a weak foul stream, pushing on may still beat waiting.

qa.q: How does high atmospheric pressure change the height of tide?
qa.a: Predictions assume about **1013 hPa**: each hectopascal above lowers the sea about a centimetre, each one below raises it. An onshore gale piles water up, an offshore one drives it out.

blocks.p: Predictions assume about 1013 hPa. Each hectopascal above lowers the sea about a centimetre, each one below raises it. An onshore gale piles water up, an offshore one drives it out. These are estimates: add margin for them, never spend it.

Offshore gale, two days: −0.3 m more

blocks.p: In most of the Mediterranean the range is a few decimetres, so weather moves the level more than the tide. The exceptions: about a metre in the northern Adriatic, more when a Sirocco blows up it, and up to two metres in the Gulf of Gabès. Narrows such as Messina have streams worth timing.
